title: Liberties
intro: Right. The whole game, from the beginning.
Black and White take turns putting a stone on an intersection -- a crossing of two lines, not a square. Once it is down it does not move again.
That is genuinely all the movement there is. Everything else follows from one idea, and the idea is called a liberty.

steps.instruction: Put a black stone anywhere you like. Move the cursor first -- the rings show the empty points it would be touching.
steps.explanation: The empty points touching a stone, up-down-left-right, are its liberties. A stone in the middle of the board has four. That number is the stone's breathing room, and the entire game is an argument about it.

steps.instruction: Now put a stone in a corner. Watch the count change.
steps.hint: Any of the four corners of the board.
steps.explanation: A corner stone has two liberties; an edge stone has three. Stones near the edge are easier to take, which is why the edge is cheap and the corner is valuable -- you need fewer stones to surround a corner than a centre.

steps.instruction: Play a third black stone directly below the other two, to make a line of three.
steps.hint: Directly under the lowest black stone.
steps.explanation: Stones of the same colour that touch are one chain, and they share their liberties. They live together and they die together. Three stones in a row have eight liberties between them -- much harder to surround than three lonely stones.

outro: That is the whole of the first lesson. Liberties belong to chains, edges have fewer of them, and corners fewer still.
Next: what happens when a chain runs out.
